steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on CrIBo, a self-supervised learning method that bootstraps object-level representations across images. Motivate it from the state of SSL in NLP vs. vision and from in-context scene understanding with dense nearest neighbor retrieval, say how it differs from existing SSL methods, and end with our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. SSL, foundation models, and the gap between NLP and computer vision
2. Contextual pretraining for dense nearest neighbor retrieval and its limitations
3. How CrIBo departs from image-level invariance SSL
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. SSL and foundation models
- AI advances driven by democratization of deep learning (cite)
- SSL = major factor in deep learning success; enables large foundation models pretrained on massive uncurated data
- NLP: large-scale task-agnostic pretraining -> general-purpose features, good on various downstream tasks
- vision: task-specific models + finetuning still de facto; partly due to no consensus on pretext task (cf. masked language modeling (MLM) in NLP)

2. Contextual pretraining (prior work, cite)
- with their contextual pretraining, dense nearest neighbor retrieval ~ task-specific models, significantly more efficient
- contextualization mechanism aligns pretraining with dense NN evaluation via within- and across-image attention
- only partial alignment: i) cross-image attention from local to global features; ii) consistency only between contextualized image-level representations of views from the same image
- our fix: explicitly enforce cross-image consistency between object-level representations (Figure 1)

3. CrIBo vs. existing SSL
- most recent SSL (cite several): image-level representations invariant to semantic-preserving augmentations
- CrIBo departs in two ways: consistency at object granularity; enforced between objects from different images
- -> pretraining aligned with general-purpose representations for dense NN retrieval
- object level -> mitigates contextual bias (cite) -> compatible with scene-centric images (bulk of web-scale datasets)

4. Contributions
- 1) first end-to-end online SSL approach explicitly enforcing cross-image consistency at object/object-part level (to our knowledge)
- 2) representations excel in in-context scene understanding (cite) without hurting standard segmentation benchmarks
- 3) compatible with scene-centric datasets; fills gap in cross-image SSL literature

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, artificial intelligence has made big advances, mostly because deep learning techniques have become democratized. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is one of the main factors behind the success of deep learning. SSL has made it possible to train large foundation models that are pretrained on massive amounts of uncurated data. In natural language processing (NLP), this large-scale task-agnostic pretraining was the key to getting general-purpose features that perform well on many different downstream tasks. In computer vision, on the other hand, task-specific models and finetuning are still the de facto choice. Part of the reason for this is that there is no consensus about the pretraining pretext task, unlike in NLP where there is masked language modeling (MLM).

Still, recent work showed that with their contextual pretraining, dense nearest neighbor retrieval performs comparably with task-specific models while being significantly more efficient. The contextualization mechanism makes sure that the pretraining phase is aligned with dense nearest neighbor evaluation, by using attention within images and across images. But this mechanism only partially fulfills the alignment objective, because i) the cross-image attention goes from local to global features and ii) consistency is only encouraged between the contextualized image-level representations of views that come from the same image. To mitigate these limitations, we propose to explicitly enforce cross-image consistency between object-level representations, as shown in Figure 1.

3. CrIBo vs. existing SSL
- most recent SSL (cite several): image-level representations invariant to semantic-preserving augmentations
- CrIBo departs in two ways: consistency at object granularity; enforced between objects from different images
- -> pretraining aligned with general-purpose representations for dense NN retrieval
- object level -> mitigates contextual bias (cite) -> compatible with scene-centric images (bulk of web-scale datasets)

4. Contributions
- 1) first end-to-end online SSL approach explicitly enforcing cross-image consistency at object/object-part level (to our knowledge)
- 2) representations excel in in-context scene understanding (cite) without hurting standard segmentation benchmarks
- 3) compatible with scene-centric datasets; fills gap in cross-image SSL literature

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, artificial intelligence has made big advances, mostly because deep learning techniques have become democratized. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is one of the main factors behind the success of deep learning. SSL has made it possible to train large foundation models that are pretrained on massive amounts of uncurated data. In natural language processing (NLP), this large-scale task-agnostic pretraining was the key to getting general-purpose features that perform well on many different downstream tasks. In computer vision, on the other hand, task-specific models and finetuning are still the de facto choice. Part of the reason for this is that there is no consensus about the pretraining pretext task, unlike in NLP where there is masked language modeling (MLM).

Still, recent work showed that with their contextual pretraining, dense nearest neighbor retrieval performs comparably with task-specific models while being significantly more efficient. The contextualization mechanism makes sure that the pretraining phase is aligned with dense nearest neighbor evaluation, by using attention within images and across images. But this mechanism only partially fulfills the alignment objective, because i) the cross-image attention goes from local to global features and ii) consistency is only encouraged between the contextualized image-level representations of views that come from the same image. To mitigate these limitations, we propose to explicitly enforce cross-image consistency between object-level representations, as shown in Figure 1.

Most recent self-supervised learning algorithms are built around the objective of learning image-level representations that are invariant to data augmentations that preserve semantics. CrIBo departs from this paradigm in two ways. First, we encourage consistency at the level of the objects in the images, and second, this consistency is enforced between objects from different images. By doing this, our pretraining is well aligned with the objective of getting general-purpose representations that are tailored for dense nearest neighbor retrieval. Also, since it works at the object level, CrIBo mitigates the pitfall of contextual bias, so it is compatible with scene-centric images, which make up the bulk of web-scale datasets.

Our contributions are the following. 1) To the best of our knowledge, CrIBo is the first end-to-end online SSL approach that explicitly enforces cross-image consistency at the object/object-part level. 2) The representations we get excel in in-context scene understanding tasks and do not compromise the performance on standard segmentation benchmarks. 3) Also, CrIBo is compatible with scene-centric datasets, which addresses a gap in the existing cross-image SSL literature.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) is one of the main factors behind the success of deep learning. SSL has made it possible to train large foundation models that are pretrained on massive amounts of uncurated data. In natural language processing (NLP), this large-scale task-agnostic pretraining was the key to getting general-purpose features that perform well on many different downstream tasks. In computer vision, on the other hand, task-specific models and finetuning are still the de facto choice. Part of the reason for this is that there is no consensus about the pretraining pretext task, unlike in NLP where there is masked language modeling (MLM).

Still, [2] showed that with their contextual pretraining, dense nearest neighbor retrieval performs comparably with task-specific models while being significantly more efficient. The contextualization mechanism makes sure that the pretraining phase is aligned with dense nearest neighbor evaluation, by using attention within images and across images. But this mechanism only partially fulfills the alignment objective, because i) the cross-image attention goes from local to global features and ii) consistency is only encouraged between the contextualized image-level representations of views that come from the same image. To mitigate these limitations, we propose to explicitly enforce cross-image consistency between object-level representations, as shown in Figure 1.

Most recent self-supervised learning algorithms [3,4,5,6] are built around the objective of learning image-level representations that are invariant to data augmentations that preserve semantics. CrIBo departs from this paradigm in two ways. First, we encourage consistency at the level of the objects in the images, and second, this consistency is enforced between objects from different images. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Over the past few years, the field of artificial intelligence has seen significant advancements, primarily driven by the democratization of deep learning techniques [1]. Self-supervised learning (SSL) stands out as one of the major factors contributing to the success of deep learning. Indeed, SSL has opened the door to training large foundation models pretrained on massive amounts of uncurated data. In natural language processing (NLP), this large-scale task-agnostic pretraining has been the key to unlocking general-purpose features that perform well on various downstream tasks. In computer vision, by contrast, task-specific models and finetuning remain the de facto choice, in part due to the lack of consensus around the pretraining pretext task, such as masked language modeling (MLM) in NLP.

Nonetheless, [2] showed that under their contextual pretraining, dense nearest neighbor retrieval performed comparably with task-specific models while being significantly more efficient. The contextualization mechanism ensures that the pretraining phase is aligned with dense nearest neighbor evaluation by leveraging within and across image attention. Nevertheless, this mechanism only partially fulfills the alignment objective, as i) the cross-image attention mechanism goes from local to global features and ii) consistency is only encouraged between contextualized image-level representations of views from the same image. To mitigate these limitations, we propose to explicitly enforce cross-image consistency between object-level representations, as shown in Figure 1.

Most recent self-supervised learning algorithms, e. g., [3,4,5,6], revolve around learning image-level representations invariant to semantic-preserving data augmentations. CrIBo departs from this paradigm in two ways. First, we encourage consistency at the granularity of the objects in the images, and second, this consistency is enforced between objects from different images. In doing so, our pretraining aligns well with the objective of obtaining general-purpose representations tailored for dense nearest neighbor retrieval. Furthermore, by operating at the object level, CrIBo mitigates the pitfall of contextual bias [7] and is therefore compatible with scene-centric images, which constitute the bulk of web-scale datasets.

Our contributions are as follows. 1) To the best of our knowledge, CrIBo is the first end-to-end online SSL approach that explicitly enforces cross-image consistency at the object/object-part level. 2) The resulting representations excel in in-context scene understanding tasks [2] without compromising performance on standard segmentation benchmarks. 3) Moreover, CrIBo is compatible with scene-centric datasets, addressing a gap in the existing cross-image SSL literature.

References:
[1] Krizhevsky et al. (2012) Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E Hinton. Imagenet classification with deep convolutional neural networks. Advances in neural information processing systems , 25, 2012.
[2] Balažević et al. (2023) Ivana Balažević, David Steiner, Nikhil Parthasarathy, Relja Arandjelović, and Olivier J Hénaff. Towards in-context scene understanding. arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.01667 , 2023.
